title: ‘Kid Detective’ Series Adaptation in the Works at Hulu (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 28, 2026 10:30am PT ‘Kid Detective’ Series Adaptation in the Works at Hulu (EXCLUSIVE) Evan Morgan will executive produce, with Rachel Kaplan exec producing via Abescon Entertainment By Joe Otterson Plus Icon Joe Otterson TV Reporter joeotterson Latest Amazon to Develop ‘Shadow Work’ Series Based on Adrienne Miller Short Story, Marc Resteghini to Produce (EXCLUSIVE) 15 minutes ago ‘Stillwater’: Amazon Series Based on Graphic Novel Casts Ben Hardy in Lead Role 30 minutes ago ‘Icebreaker’ Netflix Series Casts Daisy Jelley, Connor Simos in Lead Roles (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago See All ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Hulu is developing a series version of the 2020 movie “The Kid Detective,” Variety has learned exclusively. Evan Morgan, who wrote and directed the film, is attached as an executive producer on the project. Alex Berger will write and executive produce. Rachel Kaplan of Abescon Entertainment will also executive produce, with Jonathan Bronfman and Will Woods — who produced the film — producing the series as well. Adam Brody, who starred in “The Kid Detective,” is not attached at this time. Related Stories ‘60 Minutes’ Kicks Off Much-Scrutinized 59th Season With Old Ticks and Tricks ‘48 Hours’ Expands Use of Video Podcasting With 'Woman in the Woods' The logline for the series states, “When a missing persons case reopens the childhood murder he never solved, a washed-up former kid detective gets one last shot at proving his best days aren’t behind him.” Popular on Variety Brody starred as the titular kid detective Abe Applebaum in the film, which debuted at TIFF in 2020. The film was well-received by critics upon its release. In his review for Variety , Tomris Laffly wrote “Splendidly summoning film noir-esque vibes, classically ghastly bad guys and femme fatale types out of a whimsical small town full of grotesque mysteries, this bold and often surprisingly humorous film…grapples with themes related to murder and abuse, as well as the existential dread of its central recluse, who fell grossly short of the promising life he thought he was meant to have in his younger days.” Berger most recently worked on “CIA” at CBS as well as shows like “The Perfect Couple” at Netflix and “Quantum Leap” for NBC. His other credits include “Blindspot,” “The Mentalist,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Glenn Martin DDS.” Kaplan was previously head of scripted TV at Keshet Studios before launching Abescon studios in 2020. Under that banner, she has executive produced shows like “La Brea” at NBC and has projects in active development across a range of streamers and networks. During her time with Keshet, she shephered shows like “The Baker and the Beauty,” “Lincoln Rhyme: The Hunt for the Bone Collector,” And “Wisdom of the Crowd.” Berger is repped by UTA, A.B. Fischer, and Yorn Levine. Morgan is repped by Range and Verve. title: Dan Trachtenberg Developing Original Pic Inspired By ‘Sleeping Beauty’ At Disney
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Justin Kroll Justin Kroll Film Editor @krolljvar More Stories By Justin Margaret Qualley & Sabrina Carpenter Join Tom Holland In Fred Astaire Biopic Berlanti/Schechter Films & Yan Fisher To Produce True Crime Dramedy ‘Hang The Decorators’ At Amazon MGM Studios ‘Fake Skating’ Feature Adaptation At Sony Taps Amélie Hoeferle and Graham Campbell To Star View All September 28, 2026 10:30am Dan Trachtenberg; 'Sleeping Beauty' Getty/Disney EXCLUSIVE: After breathing new life into the Predator franchise at 20th Century, Dan Trachtenberg and Disney have found their next property to give a fresh spin on. Sources tell Deadline the Prey director is coming on to direct an original idea inspired by the classic Disney tale Sleeping Beauty . The untitled project is in early development and is inspired by the classic fairy tale, taking the story in an entirely new direction with Trachtenberg’s distinct sensibility. While plot details are being kept under wraps, Insiders add that this take has no connection to the Maleficent films starring Angelina Jolie. Trachtenberg and Raya McClendon came up with the story with Alex Anfanger and Dan Schimpf penning the script. Related Stories News Dan Trachtenberg's Untitled 'Freddy the 13th' Animated Horror Comedy Gets Release Date Festivals Dan Trachtenberg To Direct Comedy-Horror Based on Yehudi Mercado's 'Freddy The 13th' For Paramount Animation - Annecy Trachtenberg and his long time producing partner Ben Rosenblatt will produce as will Star Wars producer Michelle Rejwan. EVP of production Jessica Virtue is overseeing the project with Creative Executive Alina Mota, reporting to Disney Live Action President Daria Cercek. Watch on Deadline Trachtenberg and Disney have strong ties after he successfully helped relaunch the Predator franchise with his hit Prey, that was not only a massive success on Hulu but also heard strong critical prase as well landing an Emmy nomination for best TV movie. He followed that up with the Predator: Badlands as well as the animated Predator pic Predator: Killer of Killers for Hulu, which also has a 94% score on Rotten Tomatoes; all three of Dan’s entries hold the record for highest rated on Rotten Tomatoes in the Predator franchise. He is currently in pre-production on a top secret pic at Paramount. Anfanger and Schimp are the co-creators of the Comedy Central series Big Time In Hollywood, FL. Trachtenberg is repped by CAA, Untitled Entertainment and Johnson Shapiro Slewett and Kole, Anfanger and Schimp are repped by Mosaic, CAA, and Ginsburg Daniels Kallis. title: Strap-On and All, ‘Rose’ Puts Sandra Hüller Back in the Oscar Conversation
full_text: × Skip to main content By Seth Abramovitch Plus Icon Seth Abramovitch Senior Writer SethAbramovitch Follow Sign Up View All September 28, 2026 10:20am 'Rose,' Sandra Huller, 2026. The Match Factory/Courtesy Everett Collection The bullet that tore through Rose ‘s face now hangs around her neck. Occasionally, she raises it to her mouth and sucks on it, a small, private gesture from a woman whose survival depends on keeping nearly everything about herself private. As played by Sandra Hüller in Markus Schleinzer’s Rose , she is a veteran of the Thirty Years’ War, which devastated Central Europe from 1618 to 1648. Now she is attempting to settle into a rural German community, acquire land and build a life, all while passing as a man. The trousers grant her freedoms she could never otherwise claim. A marriage to a local woman makes the arrangement considerably more complicated. It is a performance built from watchfulness and restraint, with Hüller allowing glimpses of tenderness, fear and finally fury to emerge from beneath Rose’s carefully maintained exterior. Related Stories Movies 'Rose' Trailer: Watch a First Look at Sandra Hüller's Next Must-See Performance (Exclusive) Music MTV Video Music Awards: Taylor Swift's Record, Madonna's Domination, Snoop Dogg's Dig and More Memorable Moments The role has already earned Hüller the Silver Bear for best leading performance at this year’s Berlin International Film Festival and could bring the Anatomy of a Fall Oscar nominee back into the best actress race. Austria has selected the black-and-white drama as its international feature submission. A new trailer debuted today ahead of the film’s Dec. 11 U.S. theatrical release. In a conversation with The Hollywood Reporter , the two discussed the freedom of leaving several central questions unanswered, the homemade device that helped Hüller find the character’s physicality and why Schleinzer refused to make her undress to prove anything. *** Rose evoked several of my favorite films. I’m very drawn to this genre of hiding within gender. I thought of movies like Yentl , Boys Don’t Cry and M. Butterfly . The tension of wondering when they’ll be found out gives those films a simmering intensity. Were those some of your inspirations, Markus? MARKUS SCHLEINZER I watched all of those films, but that was the second part of the process. The first part of the process was an incident. A friend of mine called me to wish me happy birthday. At the end of the call, she said, “Listen, it’s weird. I just finished reading a book today about a woman who got executed on this very day, your birthday, about 250 years before your birth, because she was wearing pants, because she was trying to live a different life. That’s the reason why she got executed.” This was very touching to me, and it was the beginning of a very long process of research. I started on women in pants: Why had women chosen to wear pants? To gain more freedom. I think it was two to three years, this research process, in which I was able to learn about 300 women across three different centuries. These are the women who got caught, the women we are aware of, so the figures must be much bigger. The reason why these women chose this kind of life was always different. Most of them tried to avoid getting married to someone they disliked. Some wanted to avoid rape or sexual harassment. Some wanted to have access to education, like in one of the films you mentioned, Yentl . Then there were women who wanted to fight for their countries and were not allowed to do so as women, so they chose to live like men. Some women just wanted to follow their husbands into war. There were transgender people or lesbians, I think, of course, but in those days there wasn’t an idea or words for this. All very different reasons, but the goal was always the same: to have more freedom, live more freely, have the possibility to do something which is already allowed to others. And as my first two movies had dealt with the so-called outsiders of society, I thought, OK, why not do it again, proceed with this research and this time talk about the biggest group of outsiders in the world: women. It was very interesting. The interesting thing is, when it comes to cross-dressing movies with men in dresses, what they have to do to reveal their gender is take off the wig. That’s what they do mostly. And what women in trousers always have to do is … SANDRA HÜLLER Completely undress. SCHLEINZER Yeah, completely undress to prove their gender. When we started writing the script, I said, OK, I want to try writing something on this topic without the naked body, because I don’t think a story like this needs to prove it through the naked body. Why? How often do I have to fill out some form on the internet, what’s your gender, male, female, diverse, whatever, and how often have I ticked “male” without sending pics of my naked body to prove it? So this was the beginning of this project. Is it true you wrote a novel version of Rose before you wrote the screenplay? SCHLEINZER I was a casting director for 17 years and I read the traditional scripts, but I dislike the form. As an author, I get much more in contact with a person when I choose to write in prose, like a novel, because writing in that style you can discuss thoughts, you can discuss fears, whatever. This is what I like very much. We started in the early years of Rose, when she was a child, and the novel ends where the film ends. It was about 1,000 pages. And then I thought, “Okay, you idiot, no one is going to give you millions of dollars to make a 45-hour movie.” So we just skipped the first 800 pages and concentrated on the last 200 pages of the novel, because that could survive as a movie by itself. You should release that book. I’d love to see what else happened in her life. HÜLLER Yeah, Markus, just do it. Just release the book. SCHLEINZER I don’t know. I’m not this merchandising guy who does something and then has to shoot out more, more, more, more, keep the money coming. Maybe in some 20 years I will do so. Sandra, how did you approach a character as quietly complex as Rose? Was her facial scarring something you were hesitant about, or something you thought helped you find the character? HÜLLER The script was so poetic, and there was so much information in it about the emotional state of the people. It didn’t have the usual form. It was written like a poem. Even the [stage directions] came in this special [prose] form that Markus had found. So that set the inner tone for everything we did. It gave a certain tenderness to everything we did, despite the brutality of the things that are actually happening. I can only thank Markus that he wrote it in this manner, because it was so rare. It did something very special to the whole work. As for the actual deformation of Rose’s face, it took us some time to find it. I remember, Markus, that you sent me a picture of a woman who had a scar from war, very early on. So I got familiar with the thought of having something put on my face. It was a pretty interesting construction. There had to be some pulling of the face up, and it would be clipped into the hair, like with a rubber band that kept it in place, and above that would be the form of the actual hole in the face, the scar. That’s something I’d never experienced before, and I was curious how it works when you can only use half of your face, and maybe just your eyes, for the things you want to express. I find limitations in acting very interesting. They force you to choose a certain form and help you find the essence of something when you leave a lot out. I found that very, very helpful. And it was, of course, a true pleasure to be in the makeup trailer of Anette Keiser for two hours every day. So that was always a good start. And then there was also the costume, of course. Markus referenced the trousers, the boots. HÜLLER Markus, you remember, you gave me your personal shoes, which I would have loved to keep, but I didn’t. A lot of Markus’ private life is in there, and that’s something you are aware of every day when you wear these things. You’re aware of the details and of all the love that has been put in there. It was meant to disguise something, and at the same time it was meant to give a certain feeling of strength, of course, because wearing armor does something to the body. Then we find out how her “horn” [a homemade strap-on sex device] that we discover later in the film is placed on the body, and that would also help to find out how to move and all of these things. Markus is someone who cares about all of these things. It’s something I would never have had to find out alone. It’s never specified what Rose’s impulse is for passing as a man, beyond the freedom of it. Did you come to a conclusion in your own mind as to whether she was trans, or a lesbian, or just a woman who wanted more opportunities for herself? What was your take on it? HÜLLER It’s part of the story that we don’t know, and it’s part of her personal freedom that she doesn’t tell anything about it, and I respected that. That’s all I can say. And as Markus said before, this character is an essence of hundreds of female characters from that time who chose this exact path, and their choices were very different from each other. So why would we decide on one reason? And yet there is a real love story going on between you and Caro Braun’s character, which is very heartwarming to watch unfold. But one thing you never find out is how she got pregnant with their child. Did you intentionally leave that a mystery as well? SCHLEINZER Well, I did, because I didn’t want to have this. I don’t want to look at people only as victims, and giving her this story might have put her in the victim corner. I think the things that happen to us should not define us completely. HÜLLER Caro said such a beautiful thing about that pregnancy when we were talking about the film in Berlin. She chose, for herself, that it is something that happened with pleasure. And that is something I love so much about her as a person, that she is choosing this story, although we don’t know the truth. We just have to respect it. SCHLEINZER When we were working on this, I went to Caro and said, “OK, I know you cannot play this without knowing how this happened to you, so find your own story.” And the funny thing is that she came back and said yes, now she knows everything, but she didn’t give it away. I asked her, “Who is the father?” She said, “None of your business.” Every time she gets asked in interviews, she always says, “None of your business.” And this I like very much. What do we really have to know about other people? Knowing too much, or knowing something about other people, so very often turns into judging. And is this a good thing? Does judging mean understanding? I doubt it. Was Sandra always the actress you had in mind for Rose? SCHLEINZER The part was written for Sandra. When it comes to a German-speaking part like this, there’s no way not to think about Sandra. So I stalked her. I watched all the movies I could get, to get my impression of how she does it, my impression of her enormous talent. And then I had the joy of acting alongside her in a movie, Sisi & I . I was pretty bad in that movie, because all I did was look at her and try to figure out, OK, [how would she do it?] I never told her this was written for her. HÜLLER It doesn’t always help when you know. SCHLEINZER Someone can write something for you and it still is shit. So I was very, very, very happy that she said yes. Can we talk about the scene when the townspeople confront Rose and you finally lose your cool? They reduce her identity to anatomy, while she’s arguing for her right to exist on her own terms. It brought to mind the trans and anti-trans debates you read every day on social media. What did that scene mean to you when you were making it? HÜLLER Well, we can talk about it on many levels. There’s a practical level: a night shoot in the dark, in the cold, with a lot of people who probably want to go home, so you have to really do it well so you don’t waste everybody’s time. I like the idea that she is going into the confrontation in the first place. She’s not shying away from that discussion, and she’s basically asking, Markus, please correct me if I’m wrong, whether anything she’s done for the community changes if her gender were a different one. And I think that’s fair, because obviously the answer is no. The things she has contributed to the village and to the people there, what she taught them and how she showed up, don’t change in the slightest if people find out she is not a man. It’s heartbreaking to watch you have to even make that case for yourself when you’ve done so much for the community, and they still don’t care. They still want blood. SCHLEINZER You will never fit. Is this how we want to live together as a community on this planet? I don’t know what kind of future mankind has, but this is what I see so very often. This could be a win-win situation. What she’s doing there, she’s saving a life, she’s creating jobs, she’s paying people, they learn how to read and write, things like this. She’s doing what she can, and she just wants to do it within the existing community. HÜLLER But it’s not for her to decide. That’s what we learned there. THR

title: Carrie Coon Set to Receive Vancouver’s First Luminary Award (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 28, 2026 10:15am PT Carrie Coon Set to Receive Vancouver’s First Luminary Award (EXCLUSIVE) Other Luminary Award recipients are Markus Schleinzer and Leah Nelson as VIFF unveils a wide-ranging program of talks, panels and masterclasses By Katherine Brodsky Plus Icon Katherine Brodsky Latest Vancouver Film Festival Reveals 2026 Lineup: Jesse Eisenberg, Cristian Mungiu but Also Local Talent, Indigenous and Nonfiction Cinema 4 weeks ago Green Screen: British Columbia Adopts More Sustainability Practices for Production Shoots 2 years ago Telefilm Canada Focuses on Finding Fresh Voices But Faces Financing Roadblocks 3 years ago See All Fabio Lovino/HBO Carrie Coon will be the first recipient of the Vancouver International Film Festival’s new Luminary Award in the acting category, honoring excellence and dedication to the art of moving image. The “White Lotus,” “The Gilded Age,” and “The Leftovers” star is set to take part in a wide-ranging conversation following the Oct. 4 presentation. Coon also stars in “The Liberation,” which screens earlier that day at VIFF, playing a mother trying to escape the weight of her harrowing past, only to find solace in an all-women’s cult. Related Stories ‘60 Minutes’ Notches Ratings Gain Over Last Year, but Cedes Viewers From Season Premiere Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban Beyond Coon’s appearance, VIFF’s Oct. 1-11 program will feature talks, panels and masterclasses bringing filmmakers, craftspeople, producers, programmers and other industry professionals to Vancouver. The festival will also present Luminary Awards to Markus Schleinzer (“Rose”) for directing excellence and Leah Nelson (“Tangles”) for screenwriting. Popular on Variety The festival’s VIFF Talks series kicks off Oct. 3 with editor Matthew Hannam , whose recent credits include Halina Reijn’s “Babygirl” and Noah Baumbach’s “White Noise.” Hannam, who will be discussing his collaborative approach, began his career as an assistant editor in Winnipeg, working with Canadian auteurs like Guy Maddin. Producer Haley Johnson will discuss the making of “Obsession,” the independently produced film made on a shoestring budget that went on to gross over $500 million worldwide. The Oct. 4 conversation will focus on the film’s production and subsequent trajectory, including a studio bidding war following its Toronto premiere. On Oct. 5, production designers Brandon Tonner-Connolly and Matt Hyland will discuss working together to build the surreal, immersive world of Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.” The VIFF Talks series concludes Oct. 7 with Mark Mothersbaugh , DEVO co-founder and composer behind Wes Anderson’s “Rushmore,” “The Royal Tenenbaums” and “The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou,” amongst others. He’ll be in conversation with composer and former Fox studio exec Robert Kraft. This year’s masterclass programming has a distinctly international flavor. Guests include Latvian producer, writer and director Matīss Kaža , who co-wrote and produced Gints Zilbalodis’ “Flow,” which won the Academy Award for animated feature last year. Chilean producer Giancarlo Nasi , whose credits include “The Mysterious Gaze of the Flamingo,” winner of the Grand Prix at Cannes’ Un Certain Regard n 2025, will lead a session on international co-productions. Berlin-based film editor Evelyn Rack — behind the Cannes Jury Prize winner and Germany’s Oscars submission, “Sound of Falling” — will lead “Editing as Discovery: Narrative, Instinct, and the Unpredictable.” And Barcelona-born, Berlin-based audience designer Isona Admetlla will explore audience strategy and creative distribution. The panel lineup, meanwhile, brings together figures from across the festival and distribution ecosystem. “Curating Cinema in a Shifting Landscape” will feature Pamela Biénzobas , a programmer at the Locarno Film Festival, alongside VIFF documentary programmer Ruun Nuur and critic/programmer Saffron Maeve , for a discussion of how film curation is evolving. “From Festival to Marketplace: Meet the Decision Makers” will bring together Michael Robson of Elevation Pictures, Max Collister of Mubi Canada and Richelle Charkot of Game Theory Films to discuss the path from festival exposure to distribution and audiences. The Vancouver-to-international trajectory will be the focus of “From Vancouver to the World: The Making of Tangles,” featuring director Leah Nelson alongside several members of the creative team behind the animated feature. Based on Vancouver artist Sarah Leavitt’s graphic memoir, “Tangles” was selected for Cannes the best first feature Caméra d’Or at Cannes and boasts a voice cast that includes Abbi Jacobson, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Bryan Cranston, and Seth Rogen. Other panels will examine Indigenous filmmaking and narrative sovereignty, deal-making, documentary filmmaking beyond certainty, and the craft of comedy. The festival will also showcase its Composer Filmmaker Accelerator, an initiative connecting emerging composers with filmmakers through mentorship and hands-on collaboration. It is curated by three-time Emmy-nominated composer Miriam Cutler , whose credits include “RBG,” “Love Gilda,” and “Lost in La Mancha.” The 2026 CFA showcase takes place Oct. 8. Among the filmmakers and industry figures also expected at VIFF are Canadian icon Rick Hansen , actor and “School for Defectors” producer Daniel Dae Kim , and Canadian directors Matthew Rankin (“Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney”), Marie Clements (“How We Stand,” “Reclaim My Skin”) and Zach Lipovsky (“Freaks Part II”). title: Amazon to Develop ‘Shadow Work’ Series Based on Adrienne Miller Short Story, Marc Resteghini to Produce (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 28, 2026 10:15am PT Amazon to Develop ‘Shadow Work’ Series Based on Adrienne Miller Short Story, Marc Resteghini to Produce (EXCLUSIVE) By Joe Otterson Plus Icon Joe Otterson TV Reporter joeotterson Latest ‘Stillwater’: Amazon Series Based on Graphic Novel Casts Ben Hardy in Lead Role 16 minutes ago ‘Icebreaker’ Netflix Series Casts Daisy Jelley, Connor Simos in Lead Roles (EXCLUSIVE) 4 hours ago Peter Sarsgaard Joins Kenneth Branagh in Paramount+ Series ‘Laird’ 3 days ago See All Getty Images In a competitive situation, Amazon MGM Studios is set to develop a series based on the short story “Shadow Work” by Adrienne Miller, Variety has learned exclusively from sources. Miller will write the pilot for the one-hour series and serve as executive producer. Former Amazon exec Marc Resteghini will executive produce via Jack Tar Pictures, which has an overall deal at Amazon MGM Studios. According to sources, the producers fielded multiple offers before Amazon preemptively acquired it. Related Stories ‘60 Minutes’ Kicks Off Much-Scrutinized 59th Season With Old Ticks and Tricks ‘48 Hours’ Expands Use of Video Podcasting With 'Woman in the Woods' Reps for Amazon declined to comment. Popular on Variety The logline for the show states that it follows Genevieve Pearce, “an elite ghostwriter trusted with the secrets of the rich, famous, and infamous. She embeds in their worlds, excavates secrets, reshapes memories, manufactures redemption, and transforms the powerful into the people they want the world to believe they are. Because in Genevieve’s world, whoever controls the story controls reality. But as she rewrites everyone else’s stories, she’s forced to confront the first story she ever helped rewrite: her own.” Miller is the author of the novel “The Coast of Akron” as well as the memoir “In the Land of Men,” in which she describes her rise through the male-dominated magazine world to become the first female literary editor at Esquire. During her time at Esquire, the publication won the National Magazine Award for fiction. Miller is also a frequent contributor to Vogue. She is repped by Gersh and Yorn Levine. Resteghini is currently an executive producer on the Amazon series “Young Sherlock,” which received a Season 2 renewal in April . His current slate includes an animated series adaptation of the Tui T. Sutherland “Wings of Fire” books, a feature adaptation of the upcoming Lauren Oliver novel “The Girl in the Lake” in partnership with United Artists, and a series inspired by the lyrics and characters of Billy Joel’s songbook from creator David Weil and MGM Television. Prior to launching his own production banner, Resteghini was a senior creative executive at Amazon for nearly a decade. title: ‘Resident Evil’ Producer Carter Swan Developing Keenspot Comic Book ‘The Crying Boy’ For Film
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt ‘Landman’ Star James Jordan Joins Neon’s ‘They Follow’ Tom Segura Sets Preposterous Stand-Up Tour For 2027 Mind-Reading Comedian Peter Antoniou Sets 2027 Tour View All September 28, 2026 10:12am 'The Crying Boy,' Carter Swan Gilbert Flores/PMC EXCLUSIVE: As Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil prepares to cross $200M at the worldwide box office, the film’s producer Carter Swan has a new project to announce — a film adaptation of the Keenspot comic book series The Crying Boy by Niall O’Rourke & Rob Moran. Published in 2024, The Crying Boy follows a grieving widow trying to rebuild her life in Queens after the violent death of her husband. Things take a turn for the worse when she must save her young son from an even more terrifying fate, when the haunting painting of a crying child that he eerily befriends proves to be the vessel for an ancient demon that has preyed on children for millennia. Related Stories News Kate Micucci Developing Animated Series 'Toy' Based On Keenspot Comic News Zero Gravity Management Signs Keenspot, Comics Creator Behind Hit Jennifer Lopez Pic 'Marry Me' Following a Ringo Award nomination for Best Single Issue or Short Story, The Crying Boy ‘s first issue is currently in its third printing, with a deluxe collection of the series planned for 2027 via Keenspot’s book distribution deal with Simon & Schuster. Rona Mark is scripting the big-screen adaptation. Watch on Deadline The comic’s co-creator O’Rourke said, “Super excited to work with Carter Swan and develop the project. He brings an incredible amount of experience and knowledge to this. We hit it off straight away after he read the script and he was a big fan of the Keenspot comic book series.” A senior producer at PlayStation Productions for nearly eight years — through end of 2025 — Swan worked on Cregger’s Resident Evil during his time there, as well as HBO’s The Last of Us , Uncharted , Gran Turismo , Twisted Metal and Until Dawn . As an executive producer on The Last of Us , he earned Emmy nominations in 2023 and ’25. For a time the world’s largest publisher of webcomics, Keenspot was founded in 2000. The company first broke into film with the Universal rom-com Marry Me — a 2022 adaptation of one of its webcomics starring Jennifer Lopez and Owen Wilson. The company’s first animated adaptation was Grubbs , based on the comics by Max Weaver, whose voice cast included Wil Wheaton, Jerry O’Connell, Jodie Sweetin and more. Presently, Keenspot is also developing the animated adaptations Toy starring Kate Micucci and Kung Fu Legume starring Sherry Cola and Kheng Hua Tan, among other projects. Chris Crosby, comic book publisher Keenspot’s CEO, said: “ The Crying Boy has been one of Keenspot’s best-received titles and we’re ecstatic that a producer like Swan will be helping to bring it to the big screen. title: ‘Crew Girl’ Star Miku Martineau on the Show’s Love Triangle and Her Hopes for an All-Girls Team in Season 2
full_text: Sep 28, 2026 9:45am PT ‘Crew Girl’ Star Miku Martineau on the Show’s Love Triangle and Her Hopes for an All-Girls Team in Season 2 By Isabelle Farina Plus Icon Isabelle Farina Latest ‘Crew Girl’ Star Miku Martineau on the Show’s Love Triangle and Her Hopes for an All-Girls Team in Season 2 32 minutes ago Jeff Probst Says ‘Survivor’ Needs Diversity Despite Paramount’s DEI Rollbacks: ‘All Those Differences Matter in the Story’ 18 hours ago How To Watch Neil Young, Willie Nelson, Dave Matthews Band and More Perform Live at CNN’s ‘Farm Aid Music Festival’ 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Netflix Just like the training their characters had to endure, the cast of Netflix’s latest YA hit series “ Crew Girl ” attended a two-week rowing intensive in Victoria, British Columbia, Canada, before filming. The show’s lead Miku Martineau and her pack of rowers hit the open water to soak up as much information about the sport as possible. In the meantime, they developed the camaraderie and chemistry required to be teammates on and offscreen — and even had some memorable recreational races. Related Stories ‘60 Minutes’ Season Debut Sees 21% Drop in Ratings: Is NFL or CBS News to Blame? Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban In one of these high-speed competitions between co-stars and onscreen love triangle members Kyle Clark and Sam Braun, Martineau came out on top as the duo tumbled into the water repeatedly, struggling to find their seats. Popular on Variety That training has paid off, because “Crew Girl” has sat in Netflix’s English TV Top 10 since its Sept. 10 release, and the coming-of-age sports drama has already amassed more than 16 million views in its first two weeks — a “surreal” statistic, an “ecstatic” Martineau tells Variety . “It’s such a beautiful thing when you get to collaborate with so many people on one project, and for it to finally come out and for other people to enjoy it as well,” Martineau says. “Crew Girl” follows Martineau as 16-year-old Teagan Tao as she adapts to her new life after her father’s financial fraud forced her family to move across the country and back to her mother’s hometown. There, Teagan must navigate the choppy waters of her elite prep school Easton Academy and its all-boys crew team. Unwilling to give up her own rowing dreams, she finds a spot for herself as coxswain, leading the team to victory and falling in love with some of her teammates along the way. Courtesy of Netflix While Season 1 focused on Teagan navigating her place on the boys’ team, Season 2 of “Crew Girl,” which was confirmed on Tuesday , will likely focus on the creation and development of an all-girls team, especially if Martineau has anything to say about it. “I hope there is a strong sense of friendship and teamwork and mutual respect,” she says. “I think, guys aside, the female friendship that she and Brittany could potentially have through rowing could be very special and powerful.” Like her fanbase, Martineau is just as torn over Team Josh or Team Cam — but is ultimately choosing Team Teagan. “I think [Josh and Teagan] developed a very intimate and close relationship,” Martineau says. “However, with Cam, she relates to him because he’s kind of the underdog as well as her. And he’s also just such a sweetheart, but he has his own things as well. So it is like, what’s happening with this girls’ team?” As the lead actor in a YA drama, the 22-year-old felt the responsibility to try and accurately depict teenage hardships and resilience. But she also had the added weight of representing women in male-dominated sports. Courtesy of Netflix “I hope that Teagan represents just how powerful and strong women are,” Martineau says. “I hope it gives young girls who see Teagan onscreen permission to feel like it’s OK to take up space. It’s OK to be competitive and it’s OK to not back down from a challenge, even if you’re underestimated and even if you are the underdog. It’s unfortunate that we have to go the extra mile to almost earn a seat at the table. But if anyone can do it, it’s a woman.” This spotlight on women in “Crew Girl,” especially in less-mainstream sports like rowing, is what drew Martineau to the project. That, and of course, the juicy love triangle. “I love the duality of a really strong-willed woman pursuing her greatest desire while also allowing herself to be human, and that’s OK,” Martineau says. Martineau acknowledges how influential characters like Teagan and the other players on her team can be for young audiences. “When we’re very, very young, all we want to do is fit in,” Martineau says. “The media we consume, we look for things that we can relate to to feel like we’re a part of the community. So that’s why it’s important to represent a lot of communities and people of diverse backgrounds, so that it feels like the world that we are living in.” Martineau appears to be similar to Teagan in her sunny demeanor, passion for her work and determination — but she wants you to know she’s not playing herself. She prefers each character of hers to be distinctive. For her starring role as Yumeko in the 2025 Netflix original series “Bet,” Martineau rocked blunt bangs to differentiate herself from the character and for Teagan, she proposed going fully blonde. COURTESY OF NETFLIX She also had to establish mutual trust and respect with showrunner Vivian Lin and the “Crew Girl” directors. “I want to do my best job to bring the story to life,” Martineau says. “They do as well, so it’s me trusting them and them trusting me.” Before she settles back into her single scull for Season 2, Martineau is taking it day by day just like Teagan, grounding herself with long walks and self-care. “I wish I could say what else I have in store, but it’s been so full of so many blessings and it’s so amazing,” Martineau says. full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Fox News To Launch ‘The Girls’ Podcast With Network Personalities And Others As Rotating Co-Hosts Harry Smith Returning To NBC News As A Contributor ‘Saturday Night Live’ Opens Season With Riff On Donald Trump’s Need For More Time With Zohran Mamdani: “Please Let Me Stay Here With You” View All September 28, 2026 9:35am Screenshot of taxpayer-funded Donald Trump ad The Trump White House is defending spending taxpayer dollars to run a series of ads that have drawn criticism on both sides of the aisle as they resemble campaign spots. In fact, an ad featuring Trump that ran over the weekend is nearly the same as one that he posted on social media in 2023, as he was campaigning for a return to the presidency. The ad that ran over the weekend features the message, “Paid for by the U.S. Government.” The spot he posted in 2023 features the Trump campaign logo. In the spot from the weekend and from his campaign, Trump says that “this is the final battle. With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state. We will expel the warmongers from our government. We will drive out the globalists. We will cast out the communists, marxists and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media and we will liberate America from these villains, once and for all.” Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Fox News To Launch 'The Girls' Podcast With Network Personalities And Others As Rotating Co-Hosts News Harry Smith To Return To NBC News As A Contributor Steven Cheung, White House communications director, posted on X on Sunday, “Don’t let the Fake News get away with their lies about our epic Public Service Announcements that have been running on tv.” But there has been criticism from both parties. Sen. John Kennedy (R-LA) said that “you can’t spend public money to promote yourself.” He added that “I may end up with a sombrero on my head, but I also think that we ought to have a rule that no politician can have a building named after him while he’s alive.” Kennedy’s reference to a sombrero was to Trump pushing out a deepfake video last fall of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. Trump also has sought to put his name on the Kennedy Center, even though Congress designated it as a memorial to the late president. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) posted on X, “Don’t worry, using taxpayer dollars to run ominous campaign ads of the President has been done before and is completely legal… in banana republics.” About $319,000 has been spent on the spot, according to the AP, citing estimates from AdImpact. Two other spots began running last week. The White House sent out a release on Friday contending that the spots “are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action. Instead, the announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending — at home, at the border, and abroad.” Federal law bars appropriations from being used for “publicity or propaganda” purposes, but there has been some leeway for the use of taxpayer money for public service announcements on specific issues. The White House pointed to spots by the Obama administration to promote the Affordable Care Act and the Biden administration to spread the word about the Covid vaccine. But the latest Trump spot is centered on Trump himself, not a single issue, and largely mirrors the previous campaign ad . Margaret Dylus-Yukins, legal counsel for ethics at the Campaign Legal Center, said in a statement, “Federal law prohibits taxpayer resources from being used for the benefit of a candidate, political party or public official. These ads almost entirely revolve around President Trump, who is not a candidate, but who has told voters to act as if he is on the ballot in November. The latest ad is a complete republication of a 2024 Trump campaign ad, and the earlier ad echoes themes and messages that Republicans are pushing this election; neither has any apparent connection to any federal program or service.” She added, “At a minimum, this is an appalling abuse of taxpayer dollars, particularly when hundreds of millions of private dollars are already flowing into U.S. elections—and Trump has personally helped raise enormous sums from wealthy special interests for a super PAC devoted to advancing his political agenda.” The U.S. Government is up on TV with this spot — It aired nationally on FOX yesterday during Illinois at #7 Ohio State and also during Fox News Sunday this morning pic.twitter.com/8PP9FPzUZk — Medium Buying (@MediumBuying) September 27, 2026 Shawn Levy Moves To Disney’s 20th Television With Overall Deal After Netflix Stint Taylor Swift Debuts New Music Video; Winners List; Red Carpet Photos ‘Endgame’ Reissue Assembles $26M In No. 2 Late-September Frame Ever New Cuts Hit Tech Unit; Analysis Of What’s Going On With Pubcaster’s Funding Read More About: 1 Comments

title: Shawn Levy Inks Overall Deal With Disney’s 20th Television
full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All September 28, 2026 9:33am Shawn Levy Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images Logo text Prolific producer and director Shawn Levy has a new TV home. Levy and his 21 Laps Entertainment have signed a big overall deal with 20th Television, under which they’ll develop and produce new projects for the media giant’s various platforms. The deal will kick in starting in October 2027 and marks a big move for Levy and his company; he’s been based at Netflix since 2017. “Shawn has a rare ability to tell stories that are wildly entertaining and deeply human, something he’s brought to Disney across two decades,” Disney president and chief creative officer Dana Walden said in a statement. “He moves effortlessly across genres and franchises with a remarkable sense of what captures audiences and inspires passionate fandom. He’s an incredible storyteller and a true creative partner of the highest caliber, and we are thrilled to be building this next chapter together.” Related Stories Movies Lily James Horror Film 'Seasons' Lands Fall 2027 Release From Amazon MGM (Exclusive) Movies Ryan Gosling Shows Off First Footage From 'Star Wars: Starfighter,' About "a Guy From the Wrong Side of the Galaxy" The new deal is also something of a homecoming for Levy: Some of his earliest directing credits were on Disney Channel shows The Famous Jett Jackson and So Weird . “Years before I directed movies, I started my career directing and producing television episodes for Disney Channel, and I’ve always felt a kindred spirit in Disney and their storytelling ethos,” he said. “Having worked with Dana Walden over the years when we were both at Fox, I know her to be a formidable, smart and authentic person, not to mention a force of nature as an executive. Coupled with the amazing Debra OConnell, Disney Television has such an exciting era ahead, and I’m enthusiastic and inspired to produce the next wave of 21 Laps television series with the entire Disney team. I know from experience the passionate creative DNA of this place, and it honestly just feels like home.” Levy also has an existing relationship with the company, having recently wrapped filming on the next Star Wars feature film, Starfighter , starring Ryan Gosling. Levy also directed produced Deadpool & Wolverine for Marvel and 20th Century Studios and is reteaming with Gosling and Starfighter screenwriter Jonathan Tropper on a Ghost Rider movie . “Along with Shawn’s remarkable body of work in film, he’s also been one of the most prolific producers in television over the past decade,” said Disney Entertainment Television chairman Debra OConnell. “We couldn’t be more proud to welcome Shawn and the incredibly talented team at 21 Laps Entertainment.” Levy had a very fruitful tenure at Netflix, executive producing and/or directing Stranger Things (and its animated spinoff Tales From ’85 ), The Perfect Couple, All the Light We Cannot See and Shadow and Bone , among others. “I will forever cherish the incredible ride 21 Laps has had with Netflix,” Levy’s statement reads. “I am deeply grateful to Ted [Sarandos], Bela [Bajaria], Jinny [Howe] and the many talented Netflix execs with whom we have worked over the years and, of course, look forward to continuing our collaboration on the Stranger Things universe from the Duffer Brothers. As 21 Laps fortuitously heads into its 21st year, I remain gratified by all the stories we’ve gotten to tell and as hungry as ever for the ones we haven’t yet told.” Levy and 21 Laps are repped by WME and attorney Wendy Kirk of Johnson Shapiro. title: ‘The Day the Earth Stood Still’: THR’s 1951 Review
full_text: × Skip to main content By THR Staff Plus Icon THR Staff View All September 28, 2026 9:14am 1951's 'The Day the Earth Stood Still' Everett In September 1951, 20th Century-Fox ‘s sci-fi drama The Day the Earth Stood Still rolled out in theaters following its premiere opening on Sept. 18 at New York’s Mayfair Theatre (where it grossed $6,500 that day). At the beginning of the month, the film screened at the World Science Fiction Convention in New Orleans, where 250 attendees “universally acclaimed the picture.” The 92-minute feature, directed by Robert Wise, was released as Cold War fears were at the top of the headlines and was intended as a cautionary tale (decades later, the studio remade the film with Keanu Reeves and an aughts sheen in 2008). The Hollywood Reporter’s original review is below: In The Day the Earth Stood still, producer Julian Blaustein and director Robert Wise have a highly exploitable, suspensefully entertaining drama that will ride the crest of the current cycle of science films with the ease of a space ship. Adapted from a story by Henry Bates, the drama is an intriguing science fantasy, made believable by touches of genuine humor and the faint suggestion of a romance between a pretty American widow and a mysterious visitor from another planet. The overtones of social significance are adroitly handled and make real sense in an era of tragic international quarrels. Physically, the production is all science saga should be — Blaustein supervises the special effects with telling results; the Washington locale is excellently fulfilled; and the thoughtful choice of actors accounts for convincing performances throughout. Wise’s direction imbues the narrative with the compelling atmosphere of the documentary; he creates an illusion of presenting the real thing rather than a fictional motion picture. Inevitably, the Wise technique heightens suspense values and writes terrific punch into the action scenes involving a powerful robot who accompanies the human visitor to the U.S. Michael Rennie is the visitor, a man who whirls into the center of Washington in a space ship accompanied by his robot. His mission is one of peace — he wants to talk to the President. An hysterical soldier shoots him, Rennie is carried to Walter Reed Hospital. Here, by administering medicine brought from his outer-planet home, Rennie recovers. He tells the President’s secretary that he wishes to speak to representatives of all nations on earth. The secretary informs him this is impossible. Rennie casually leaves the hospital, takes a room in a boarding house where he meets Patricia Neal and her young son, Billy Gray. His adventures with the lad are amusing; one includes a visit to Sam Jaffe’s home where, by working an intricate scientific problem within seconds, he identifies himself as a super-intellect. Jaffe agrees to bring men of science from the four corners of the globe to hear him speak. Meanwhile the police are searching frantically for him. Though wounded again, he escapes to his ship and before flying off tells those who hear him that the world must solve its petty political problems; otherwise, action by other planets in the universe will destroy the world. Rennie’s quiet dignity in the part of the space visitor brings conviction to the interesting role. Miss Neal is vibrant and lovely as the young widow, and Hugh Marlowe is vigorous as her ambitious suitor. Jaffe’s scientist is portrayed with the actor’s usual resourcefulness. Gray is fine as the youth. Supporting players include some of Hollywood’s best character actors. Commentators Drew Pearson, Gabriel Heatter, H.V. Kaltenborn and Elmer Davis are on deck to implement the air of authenticity. Leo Tover’s work in the trick photographic department is exceptional. Lyle Wheeler and Addison Hehr, allowing imagination to run wild, perform a superb job of art direction. Bernard Herrman’s eerie score and the editing of William Reynolds are other outstanding contributions to the success of the production. — Staff byline, originally published on Sept. 4, 1951. HardScope , founded by Matt Kalish, is a media company with an in-house studio built around creator-led IP. The brand is launching its YouTube channel on Sept. 30 with a slate of digital series. The company’s goal is to create original franchises that can be developed into something larger — brand partnerships, live experiences, licensing and distribution beyond HardScope’s own channels. As an incentive to grow the franchises, creators participate as equity partners in the IP they help build. The studio team includes creative executives that helped push FaZe Clan to become a global force in online gaming culture. Related Stories Major TV Networks Suspend White House Pool Coverage of Trump in Protest of His CNN Ban ‘48 Hours’ Expands Use of Video Podcasting With 'Woman in the Woods' “We’re here to bring ambitious projects to life,” said Kalish, who also serves as CEO of HardScope. “We believe that working hand-in-hand with creators as business partners is how the future of media and IP will be made, grown and scaled.” Popular on Variety HardScope’s first batch of series are set to debut between September and November, backed by nearly $4 million in production and development investment. The shows include “R3born With N3on,” which will take viewers inside the streamer’s fitness transformation, and “Unpacked With Matcrackz,” a collectibles-themed project which will see celebrity guests hunt down their most-wanted piece of memorabilia. Plus, there’s “Love & Justice With Zach Justice,” in which the host will hear both sides of a relationship issue and deliver a verdict, and “Small World With Bloody Osiris,” a global travel show that explores “what happens when a New York fashion icon goes on the hunt for the perfect outfit and location for a fit-pic.” “Creators have given the world more great content to watch than ever before, and somehow we’re choosing less of what we actually watch,” said Lars Bengston, chief content officer of HardScope. “As algorithm fatigue sets in, taste and curation start to matter a lot more. title: Ohio House of Horrors Doc Set At Oxygen
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Peter White Peter White Executive Editor, Television @peterzwhite More Stories By Peter ‘SNL’s Weekend Update Mocks Paramount+, ‘Spider-Man’, ‘The Odyssey’ & ‘Obsession’ ‘SNL’ Season 52 Premiere Delayed In Many Areas Due To College Football ‘SNL’ Promotes Keri Powers & Rebecca Schwartz View All September 28, 2026 9:00am Oxygen EXCLUSIVE : In June, in rural Ohio, 16 children, from toddlers to teenagers were found living in a 12×12 room in conditions so deplorable that authorities described it as “pure evil”. This story is set to be explored in a new feature-length documentary for Oxygen . The Versant-owned cable network has greenlit The Siders 16: Ohio House of Horrors (w/t) from KT Studios , the company behind Amazon’s Murder 101 and Peacock’s The Idaho Student Murders. The Siders 16: Ohio House of Horrors will explore the case as it unfolds in real time after the children’s parents Gary Siders Jr. and Elizabeth Siders, and their grandparents, Gary Siders Sr. and Christina Siders, were arrested at the scene. Related Stories Cancellations and Renewals Lisa Vanderpump To Host 'Snapped' Spinoff 'Rich Bitch Rampage' For Oxygen As Part Of Versant Slate News Inside Versant's Content Strategy: True-Crime, A.I., Recognizable Drama IP & More Reality Shows With Wrestlers The group were charged were multiple counts of endangering children, while, in August, Gary Siders Jr. and Elizabeth were also charged with allegations of child sexual abuse in a separate case. Watch on Deadline The film will touch on these unexpected new charges and ask: Who ultimately bears responsibility for what happened to these children? The 90-minute doc will premiere later this year on Oxygen True Crime. It follows the success of The Hooters Murders: Deadly Shift, which was Oxygen’s most-watched doc premiere in more than two years. The Siders 16: Ohio House of Horrors is directed by KT Studios founder Stephanie Lydecker, who also exec produces alongside Kevin Brennecke. Alongside the doc, the network will also launch its first-ever companion podcast series. The ten-part audio series will be available on all major podcast platforms as well as Oxygen’s digital platforms. title: ‘Wildwood’ Studio Laika Is First Honoree For This Year’s Gotham Film Awards
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Patrick Hipes Patrick Hipes Executive Managing Editor More Stories By Patrick Santa Barbara Film Festival Awards: ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Star John Malkovich To Get Performer Of The Year Honor ‘Madden’ Trailer: Boom! Russell’s Biopic Of NFL Icon ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Trailer: Martin McDonagh’s Venice Hit Saddles Up For Awards-Season Run View All September 28, 2026 9:00am 'Wildwood' Laika EXCLUSIVE: Laika , the animation studio that has scored six Oscar nominations for its stop-motion films including Coraline, ParaNorman, The Boxtrolls and Kubo and Two Strings since its founding in 2005, will be honored with the Gotham Anniversary Tribute at this year’s Gotham Film Awards . The tribute commemorates Laika’s 20 years of storytelling and the release of Wildwood , its newest film, which hits theaters October 23 via Fathom Entertainment. The pic will have its world premiere at the London Film Festival October 11 and 10 days later serve as the opening-night film at AFI Fest . Related Stories Trailers Laika Unveils Final Trailer For Latest Stop-Motion Fantasy Adventure ‘Wildwood’ Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Guilds & More It marks the first tribute award revealed for the 36th annual Gothams, put on by the Gotham Film & Media Institute, which take place this year November 20 at Cipriani Wall Street in New York City. Watch on Deadline “After 20 years of pushing the boundaries of modern cinema and animation, this moment feels like both a celebration and an evolution for Laika,” said Jeffrey Sharp, executive director of the institute, which earlier this year teamed with the animation studio to launch Laika x Gotham Animation Accelerator for creators working on animated short films. “With Wildwood , Laika’s most ambitious film to date, and the launch of Laika Live Action opening up new creative territory, the studio continues to expand the possibilities of what handcrafted storytelling can be. We can think of no more fitting honoree for this year’s Anniversary Tribute, and we’re thrilled to welcome the Laika team to celebrate with us.” Travis Knight, Laika’s president and CEO, directs Wildwood , which was written by Chris Butler based on Colin Meloy’s novel. It centers on headstrong teenager Prue McKeel (Peyton Elizabeth Lee), who after her baby brother is abducted by a murder of crows launches with her hapless but loyal classmate Curtis Mehlberg (Jacob Tremblay) a rescue mission into the Impassable Wilderness — an enchanted forest hidden just beyond Portland, OR. It voice cast also includes Carey Mulligan, Mahershala Ali, Angela Bassett, Awkwafina, Jake Johnson, Charlie Day, Amandla Stenberg, Jemaine Clement, Maya Erskine, Tantoo Cardinal, Tom Waits and Richard E. Grant. “We’re deeply honored that The Gotham is recognizing Laika at a moment when we’re celebrating two decades of filmmaking and bringing Wildwood to audiences,” said David Burke, Laika’s Chief Marketing & Operations Officer. “Our partnership on the Laika x Gotham Animation Accelerator reflects something we care deeply about: creating meaningful opportunities for bold new voices to push animation forward. We’re grateful to The Gotham for this recognition and for a partnership grounded in a shared belief in original, ambitious storytelling.” More Gotham tributes will be rolled out throughout the fall, with nominations in the 10 competition Gotham Awards categories to be revealed October 27. title: Daisy Jelley and Connor Simos Tapped to Lead Netflix Hockey Romance ‘Icebreaker’
full_text: Skip to main content By Nicole Fell Plus Icon Nicole Fell Associate Editor nicolemfell Follow Sign Up View All September 28, 2026 8:15am Connor Simos and Daisy Jelley Sally Flegg; Lily Craigen Logo text Netflix has founds the Icebreaker leads. Daisy Jelley ( Poser , How to Have Sex ) and Connor Simos ( Subversion ) have been cast as Anastasia “Stassie” Allen and Nate Hawkins, the streamer announced Monday. The show, based on Hannah Grace’s best-selling romance novel of the same name, centers around the relationship between a college hockey player and a college figure skater. The novel is the first in Grace’s college-set Maple Hills series and is one of, if not the, most recognizable title in the hockey romance sub-genre. Related Stories Movies 'Unabomber' Review: Jacob Tremblay and Russell Crowe in a Facile Rendering of Ted Kaczynski's College Days TV Felicia Pride on Capturing Innocence, Humanity in 'A Different World' Sequel and Revering the Original: "We're Not Replacing It" The show’s synopsis reads, “The upcoming college romance series follows Anastasia Allen, a competitive figure skater with her eyes on Olympic gold. Everything changes when Anastasia is forced to share the rink with Nate Hawkins, a hockey player who’s equally determined to go pro. Despite the cold temperatures on the ice, the heat between Anastasia and Nate is undeniable. Is ambition or attraction the sharper blade?” Amanda Lasher ( Gossip Girl, The Bold Type ) will serve as the showrunner. She’ll co-write and execute produce the series alongside Jade Bartlett, who’s created as the creator. Alex Cooper’s Unwell Productions is executive producing the series with Cooper, Matt Kaplan and Meena Lefevre also serving as EPs. Grace also serves as an executive producer on the project. The greenlight comes on the heels of two successful hockey romance series at other streamers. Crave and HBO Max’s Heated Rivalry kicked off the wave on television (it’s long been popular in the romance novel space) in November. The show, which follows the decade-long romance between two rival hockey players, became a global hit and launched its two stars, Hudson Williams and Connor Storrie, into the spotlight. It’s set to return in 2027 for its second season. Earlier this summer, Prime Video released its foray into hockey romance, Off Campus , which became the streamer’s third biggest debut ever. The buzzy show, centered around a college hockey team and the women in their lives, is currently shooting its second season, which will feature a new couple — played by Mika Adballa and Stephen Kalyn — in the leading roles. title: What Will David Ellison Name His Mega Hollywood Studio?
full_text: × Skip to main content By Erik Hayden Plus Icon Erik Hayden Executive Editor, Business Erik_Hayden Follow Sign Up View All September 28, 2026 6:12am David Ellison already likes the Skydance Corporation name. Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images Bigger-is-better studio merger logic goes back in Hollywood nearly as long as the industry has existed. So, too, do eyerolls about such consolidation. In 1933, for instance, comedy troupe the Marx Brothers unveiled the name of their production company, with a characteristic wink , as International Amalgamated Consolidated Affiliated World Wide Film Productions Company Incorporated, of North Dakota. That name makes saying aloud “ Paramount Skydance Warner Bros. Discovery ” seem like almost like a breeze after the final ink is dry on David Ellison’s $111 billion merger. But, for this day and age, even five words — a mashup of two century-old studio names on each side of an upstart new media company, with a cable channel tacked on at the end — seem like too much. That’s the dilemma facing Team Ellison: What does he name a company that just seemingly vacuumed up half of Hollywood? Up until now it’s been known as WarnerMount, which tellingly leads with the acquired studio, or ParaBros, which is more of a nod to the optics of the C-suite mix of the buyers. But the formal name has yet to be unveiled and Paramount is staying mum, declining comment on that. But the name is no small thing. The decision will signal to both the industry and the Wall Street crowd what its new owner prioritizes. On a big picture scale, you could say it sets the strategic direction. Does Ellison want to look forward, rather than backward, given all of his talk about taking on tech giants in the attention economy? Or does his love of the entertainment industry, and big-budget moviemaking, nod to a nostalgic side? And now, with a rules-of-the-road consent decree to abide by thanks to California attorney general Rob Bonta, he’s got to keep in mind the optics for that crew as well (You can’t look like a monopoly right after closing a deal where the primary complaint from critics is that the merger vaporizes another buyer from the landscape). And the titling will also tip to how Ellison’s own ego plays in to the process, too. The Paramount Pictures logo, circa 1989 when Gulf and Western Inc. changed its name to Paramount Communications. Everett The Warner Bros. logo during its Time Warner days. Everett There’s tradition to think of. The Paramount Pictures name and script typeface conjures up Oscars’ best picture winners like The Godfather or Forrest Gump or Top Gun . That’s the reason why, after Shari Redstone re-merged her father Sumner’s Viacom and CBS empires, she rebranded the robotic and clunkily named ViacomCBS as Paramount Global, alongside christening its flagship streamer Paramount+ (and ditching that CBS All Access name). The Paramount name, Redstone believed, signaled quality and Classic Hollywood, and was a known commodity worldwide. The same could be said about Warner Bros., home of Casablanca and Rebel Without a Cause and countless other classics (many of which we associate with Warners but are actually MGM features, like Wizard of Oz , thanks to Warners buying much of that library and playing those movies on rotation on the Turner Classic Movies channel). It’s the reason why the Warner name has stuck around despite countless mergers and acquisitions. It weathered a merger with then-publishing giant Time Inc and suffered the indignity of having AOL take it over in what’s now regarded as the most disastrous media megadeal of all-time. In what probably should’ve been a tell, when AT&T acquired it in 2018, the telecom swallowed Time Warner whole and there was no trace of the Warner name. Deemed immaterial to AT&T just a few years later, it was spun out to David Zaslav’s cable giant, who — in arguably a nod to his ego — made sure that Discovery was represented in the Warner Bros. Discovery merger. That framing made it seem like Warner Bros. and Discovery were equals, when in reality the assets that were sought after (like the movie studio and HBO) were mostly all on the WB side. Zaslav’s team tried a stab at that Golden Age of Hollywood quality when revealing a truly hideous logo in 2021 alongside a quote from The Maltese Falcon (“The stuff that dreams are made of”). Yes, this was a real logo , circa 2021, for Warner Bros. Discovery. But by the time the company closed in 2022 it was consigned to the trash bin. One clue as to how Ellison may look to go about the naming is what he did when his far-smaller Skydance Media (Est. 2006) merged with Paramount (Est. 1912). Remember, when Skydance first inked a deal in 2024 nearly a year before closing on Paramount it initially redesigned the Paramount logo to look like the Skydance one. As if that Skydance DNA would be what turbocharged the next chapter of Paramount. In an investor presentation , Skydance’s team initially redesigned the classic Paramount logo with the Skydance font. Paramount Skydance That change ultimately didn’t take when the deal closed — why mess with a font synonymous with Hollywood? The Paramount script has been around nearly as long as the company existed. It’s been replicated on venues far from Los Angeles and has been the first thing that audiences have seen on countless titles in theaters (the Indiana Jones movies come to mind as far as how each first scene finds a way to play off the Paramount mountain). There’s an authenticity test here. That Skydance-ified Paramount logo looks just a bit off , especially for a studio that’s been around 100 years. Here’s the Paramount Pictures logo adorning the front gate of the Hollywood studio lot in 1920: The front gate to Paramount Studios in 1920. If you squint, it could be 2026 except for that car driving through the gate. Getty Images While formally the company is now titled Paramount Skydance (i.e. framed as a marriage of equals even though it’s really not), just take a look at the water tower on the lot to see how Ellison is really playing it. The tower has the iconic Paramount mountain, stars and script font with just a small disclaimer underneath that says “A Skydance Corporation.” Should we expect that for the Warner Bros. water tower in Burbank soon as well? It seems like a decent bet. Is “A Skydance Corporation” the biggest hint to how Ellison is approaching these names? Mario Tama/Getty Images In that case, when the deal formally closes, presumably in early October, will Ellison ultimately unveil Skydance Corporation as the new name for his entire holding company that houses dozens of cable channels along with two movie studios and two major news brands? HBO, a Skydance Corporation. CNN, a Skydance Corporation. Paramount has been there before, too, when it was snapped up by manufacturing conglomerate Gulf and Western Industries in 1966 and got labeled “A Gulf + Western Company” underneath its logo. There’s some organizing logic there for synergy when labeling a far-flung empire of assets. There’s a few problems with that. First, Skydance is the least iconic of all the names that Ellison has collected so far. Yes, it’s his own company that he boot-strapped and built himself (well, boot-strapped and built with financial help from his father, Oracle mogul Larry Ellison, who’s worth around $200 billion). But, optically, nothing says “I bought and ingested iconic studios and now they’re just tiles on a screen in my holding company” like wiping out the studio names from the parent company’s business card. Second, this new company isn’t AT&T, which ultimately cared far more about the telecom side of things and was fine jettisoning Warner because it wasn’t a core part of its business. Movies and television shows are the name of the game for this merged company. So you’d guess, then, that you should put your best foot forward by leading with the most recognizable, blue-chip names. Think back to all the handwringing and embarrassing reversals during the AT&T and Warner Bros. Discovery years as to whether the flagship streamer should be named Max or HBO Max. (It started off as HBO Max before turning in to Max and then going back to its original name HBO Max.) Ultimately, the C-suite led with the name that signaled quality to the widest set of possible consumers (even if execs privately fretted about diluting the good name of HBO with a streaming service featuring thousands of shows of varying quality). In this instance, if Ellison does indeed name his holding company Skydance Corporation it may be the Max of all the options, even if it doesn’t tip his hat in favor of any particular studio aside from the one that he started himself. Right now, the company trades as PSKY on the Nasdaq, though it’s set to move to the New York Stock Exchange in early October. (The symbol, SKY, it should be noted, is already taken on the NYSE by a modular home manufacturing company.) If including Skydance Corporation in the main part of the name is indeed the plan, maybe going the Marx Bros.’ “Amalgamated Consolidated Affiliated…” approach with the studio names would’ve been the better call, after all, to keep a piece of Hollywood history preserved. The Hollywood Reporter ‘s front page on March 11, 1933, which included an item about the Marx Bros. naming their company the International Amalgamated Consolidated Affiliated World Wide Film Productions Company Incorporated, of North Dakota. title: Italy’s Fandango Distribution Acquires Zurich Doc Jury President’s ‘Rescue’, RTS Joins as Broadcaster (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 28, 2026 5:30am 'Rescue' Troels N´Koya Jensen Italy’s Fandango Distribution has acquired Sine Plambech’s Rescue for all rights, including theatrical release, The Hollywood Reporter has learned. Radio Télévision Suisse (RTS) has come on board as a broadcaster, joining pre-sale partners DR, VPRO, SVT and NRK, in deals negotiated by Vienna-based Autlook Filmsales, which handles worldwide sales on the film. The agreements land as Plambech, serving as president of the documentary competition jury at the 22nd Zurich Film Festival , presents the European premiere of Rescue in the festival’s Now/Future section this week. Related Stories Movies Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival's 30th Anniversary Edition to Open With Cannes Film 'Ulya' Movies Casey Affleck on Matt Damon Rivalry, a Chris Nolan Phone Call and Being a Proud "Hollywood Outsider" Rescue tells the story of Roro, a Yemeni mother of young children fighting to reunite her family after a Mediterranean rescue operation left her separated from her husband and held in captivity in Libya. Filmed with rare access aboard Doctors Without Borders’ Geo Barents, the documentary examines the fallout of Europe’s “externalization” of migration control to North African countries, tracing one woman’s fight for justice, dignity and the right to be seen amid a broken system. The film is written by Plambech and Janus Metz, and produced by Elk Film’s Andreas Dalsgaard, Sofie Husum Johannesen, and Tereza Šimíková. Troels N’koya Jensen is the cinematographer, with editing by Per K. Kirkegaard and Marion Tuor and music by Uno Helmersson. Running 80 minutes, the film is in Arabic, English and French with English subtitles. Rescue had its world premiere at TIFF and screens in Zurich’s Now/Future section, which this year features nine films exploring human rights, social conflict and sustainable development. Presented in collaboration with the EurAsia Heart Foundation and Dementia Research Switzerland, the section highlights figures committed to equality and social justice alongside perspectives on ecological, social and economic questions for the future. Plambech is currently heading up the doc competition jury in Zurich. She is an award-winning director, anthropologist and senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS). Among other things, she directed Mission Trafficking (2010, in collaboration with Judith Lansade) and Becky’s Journey (2014), and provided the research foundation for From Thailand to Thy (2008) and From Thy to Thailand (2008), both directed by Janus Metz. Her major breakthrough, Heartbound (2018), which built upon the two films from 2008, had its world premiere at TIFF, was selected for IDFA, and won the Golden Eye Award for best international documentary at the Zurich Film Festival that year.
